definition: Idealistic in a noble, romantic way but wildly unrealistic or impractical.
example: Her quixotic plan to restore the old canal using only volunteers charmed the town but stalled within a year.
nuance: Unrealistic just means unlikely to work; quixotic adds a lofty, generous motive, so the folly is admirable rather than foolish.
prompt: A retired teacher announces a goal for her small hometown library.
options: Her quixotic goal was for every child in the county to read a thousand books by age ten.
Her quixotic plan was to replace the cracked shelves this spring before any of them collapsed.
She filled the reading room with quixotic plants imported from distant rainforests.
Her quixotic scheme was to quietly raise late fees and keep the extra money herself.
reasons: A generous ambition far beyond what one small library can achieve is noble but impractical.
Fixing a clear, achievable problem on schedule is sensible, not a lofty dream.
This confuses the word with exotic; it describes impractical ideals, not faraway origins.
A selfish, calculated scheme lacks the high-minded idealism the word requires.

practice.prompt: A young engineer talks about what he hopes to build after graduating.
options: His quixotic aim was to cut corners on safety so his firm could earn more each quarter.
He was so quixotic that he finished the exam twenty minutes before anyone else.
His quixotic dream was to give away a solar water pump to every farm on the continent.
His quixotic approach was to copy a proven design and stay strictly within the budget.
reasons: Profit-driven corner cutting is cynical, with none of the noble idealism implied.
The word has nothing to do with being quick; it describes lofty, unworkable ideals.
A kind-hearted vision on an impossible scale captures the romantic impracticality.
Relying on tested methods and tight budgets is cautious realism, the reverse of the word.
